claim: Spontaneous fluctuations of neural activity may explain why sensory responses vary across repeated presentations of the same physical stimulus.
source: Spontaneous fluctuations of neural activity may explain why sensory responses vary across repeated presentations of the same physical stimulus.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the abstract that frames the research question.

claim: Strong prestimulus alpha- and beta-band power resulted in a suppression of early ERP components (C1 and N150).
source: We found that strong prestimulus alpha- and beta-band power resulted in a suppression of early ERP components (C1 and N150) and in an amplification of late components (after 0.4 s), even after controlling for fluctuations in 1/f aperiodic signal and sleepiness.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract and supported by experimental data presented in the results section.

claim: Strong prestimulus alpha- and beta-band power resulted in an amplification of late ERP components (after 0.4 s).
source: We found that strong prestimulus alpha- and beta-band power resulted in a suppression of early ERP components (C1 and N150) and in an amplification of late components (after 0.4 s), even after controlling for fluctuations in 1/f aperiodic signal and sleepiness.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: The effects of prestimulus power on ERP components persist even after controlling for fluctuations in 1/f aperiodic signal and sleepiness.
source: We found that strong prestimulus alpha- and beta-band power resulted in a suppression of early ERP components (C1 and N150) and in an amplification of late components (after 0.4 s), even after controlling for fluctuations in 1/f aperiodic signal and sleepiness.
evidence: This is a finding that demonstrates the robustness of the main effects after controlling for potential confounds.

claim: Functional inhibition of sensory processing underlies the reduction of early ERP responses.
source: Whereas functional inhibition of sensory processing underlies the reduction of early ERP responses, we found that the modulation of non-zero-mean oscillations (baseline shift) accounted for the amplification of late responses.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data based on the functional inhibition account, supported by experimental findings.

claim: The modulation of non-zero-mean oscillations (baseline shift) accounted for the amplification of late responses.
source: Whereas functional inhibition of sensory processing underlies the reduction of early ERP responses, we found that the modulation of non-zero-mean oscillations (baseline shift) accounted for the amplification of late responses.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation supported by experimental data on non-zero-mean oscillations and baseline shift.

claim: Spontaneous neural activity can explain a substantial amount of the trial-by-trial variability in perceptual and cognitive performance.
source: Numerous studies have shown that such spontaneous neural activity can explain a substantial amount of the trial-by-trial variability in perceptual and cognitive performance (e.g., Haegens et al., 2011; Myers et al., 2014; Iemi et al., 2017) and that abnormalities in spontaneous neural activity serve as biomarkers for neuropathologies (e.g., in schizophrenia, Parkison's disease, and Autism Spectrum Disorder; Uhlhaas and Singer, 2010; McCarthy et al., 2011; Simon and Wallace, 2016) and aging (Voytek et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Abnormalities in spontaneous neural activity serve as biomarkers for neuropathologies (e.g., in schizophrenia, Parkison's disease, and Autism Spectrum Disorder).
source: Numerous studies have shown that such spontaneous neural activity can explain a substantial amount of the trial-by-trial variability in perceptual and cognitive performance (e.g., Haegens et al., 2011; Myers et al., 2014; Iemi et al., 2017) and that abnormalities in spontaneous neural activity serve as biomarkers for neuropathologies (e.g., in schizophrenia, Parkison's disease, and Autism Spectrum Disorder; Uhlhaas and Singer, 2010; McCarthy et al., 2011; Simon and Wallace, 2016) and aging (Voytek et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on neuropathologies.

claim: Abnormalities in spontaneous neural activity serve as biomarkers for aging.
source: Numerous studies have shown that such spontaneous neural activity can explain a substantial amount of the trial-by-trial variability in perceptual and cognitive performance (e.g., Haegens et al., 2011; Myers et al., 2014; Iemi et al., 2017) and that abnormalities in spontaneous neural activity serve as biomarkers for neuropathologies (e.g., in schizophrenia, Parkison's disease, and Autism Spectrum Disorder; Uhlhaas and Singer, 2010; McCarthy et al., 2011; Simon and Wallace, 2016) and aging (Voytek et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Voytek et al., 2015.

claim: The mechanisms by which spontaneous neural activity impacts the processing of sensory information remain unknown.
source: Yet, the mechanisms by which spontaneous neural activity impacts the processing of sensory information remain unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge that motivates the study.

claim: Early ERP components (<0.200 s) are thought to be generated by an activation of sensory brain areas adding on top of ongoing activity (additive mechanism).
source: ERP components occurring during the early time window (<0.200 s) are thought to be generated by an activation of sensory brain areas adding on top of ongoing activity (additive mechanism: Bijma et al., 2003; Shah et al., 2004; Mäkinen et al., 2005; Mazaheri and Jensen, 2006).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Early ERP components are associated with an increase in the magnitude of multi-unit activity (MUA) in sensory areas.
source: Invasive studies in non-human primates demonstrated that early ERP components are associated with an increase in the magnitude of multi-unit activity (MUA) in sensory areas (Kraut et al., 1985; Schroeder et al., 1990; Schroeder et al., 1991; Schroeder et al., 1998; Shah et al., 2004; Lakatos et al., 2007), presumably as a result of membrane depolarization due to excitatory synaptic activation (Schroeder et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to invasive studies in non-human primates.

claim: The increase in MUA associated with early ERP components is presumably a result of membrane depolarization due to excitatory synaptic activation.
source: Invasive studies in non-human primates demonstrated that early ERP components are associated with an increase in the magnitude of multi-unit activity (MUA) in sensory areas (Kraut et al., 1985; Schroeder et al., 1990; Schroeder et al., 1991; Schroeder et al., 1998; Shah et al., 2004; Lakatos et al., 2007), presumably as a result of membrane depolarization due to excitatory synaptic activation (Schroeder et al., 1995).
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism, supported by a citation.

claim: Early ERP components (e.g., C1) are associated with an increase in the hemodynamic fMRI signal in visual areas.
source: Non-invasive studies in humans showed that early ERP components (e.g., C1) are associated with an increase in the hemodynamic fMRI signal in visual areas (Di Russo et al., 2002), which may reflect an additive sensory response.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a non-invasive study in humans.

claim: The increase in hemodynamic fMRI signal associated with early ERP components may reflect an additive sensory response.
source: Non-invasive studies in humans showed that early ERP components (e.g., C1) are associated with an increase in the hemodynamic fMRI signal in visual areas (Di Russo et al., 2002), which may reflect an additive sensory response.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the fMRI findings.

claim: Low-frequency neural oscillations are thought to set the state of the neural system for information processing.
source: Low-frequency neural oscillations are thought to set the state of the neural system for information processing (Klimesch et al., 2007; Jensen and Mazaheri, 2010; Mathewson et al., 2011; Spitzer and Haegens, 2017), which in turn may modulate the generation of additive ERP components.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim supported by citations.

claim: The slow ERP component, which becomes visible during the late time window (>0.200 s), is generated by a modulation of ongoing oscillatory power, rather than by an additive response.
source: According to the baseline-shift account, the slow ERP component, which becomes visible during the late time window (>0.200 s), is generated by a modulation of ongoing oscillatory power, rather than by an additive response (Nikulin et al., 2007; Nikulin et al., 2010a; Mazaheri and Jensen, 2008; Mazaheri and Jensen, 2010; van Dijk et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim from the baseline-shift account, supported by citations.

claim: Neural oscillations do not vary symmetrically around the zero line of the signal, but rather around a non-zero offset/mean.
source: In contrast to this traditional view, recent studies (Nikulin et al., 2007; Nikulin et al., 2010a; Mazaheri and Jensen, 2008; van Dijk et al., 2010; Schalk, 2015; Cole and Voytek, 2017) proposed that neural oscillations do not vary symmetrically around the zero line of the signal, but rather around a non-zero offset/mean (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Trial averaging does not eliminate non-phase-locked oscillations with a non-zero mean.
source: Accordingly, trial averaging does not eliminate non-phase-locked oscillations with a non-zero mean.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of oscillations having a non-zero mean.

claim: Any amplitude modulation of oscillations with a non-zero mean is expected to change the signal baseline (baseline shift).
source: As a consequence, any amplitude modulation of oscillations with a non-zero mean is expected to change the signal baseline (baseline shift), and will therefore affect the ERP amplitude.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the properties of non-zero-mean oscillations.

claim: During event-related desynchronization (ERD) of low-frequency oscillations, the power suppression is expected to cause a slow shift of the signal baseline toward the zero line.
source: Specifically, during the event-related desynchronization (ERD) of low-frequency oscillations, the power suppression is expected to cause a slow shift of the signal baseline toward the zero line.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the baseline-shift mechanism.

claim: An ERD of oscillations with a negative non-zero-mean is expected to generate an upward slow shift of the ERP.
source: In particular, an ERD of oscillations with a negative non-zero-mean is expected to generate an upward slow shift of the ERP (and viceversa).
evidence: This is a specific prediction of the baseline-shift mechanism.

claim: States of strong prestimulus power would yield a strong ERD.
source: Accordingly, we predicted that states of strong prestimulus power would yield a strong ERD (Min et al., 2007; Becker et al., 2008; Tenke et al., 2015; Benwell et al., 2018), resulting in an enhancement of the slow ERP component during the late time window.
evidence: This is a prediction supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Strong prestimulus power results in an enhancement of the slow ERP component during the late time window.
source: Accordingly, we predicted that states of strong prestimulus power would yield a strong ERD (Min et al., 2007; Becker et al., 2008; Tenke et al., 2015; Benwell et al., 2018), resulting in an enhancement of the slow ERP component during the late time window.
evidence: This is a prediction that is tested and confirmed by the experimental data.

claim: The C1 component peaked on average at 0.079 s (SEM = 0.001) for LVF stimuli.
source: On stimulation trials, the C1 component peaked on average at 0.079 s (SEM = 0.001) and at 0.078 s (SEM = 0.001) for LVF and UVF stimuli respectively, with a maximum at occipito-parietal electrodes (Figure 2B, left and middle panels).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experimental data.

claim: The C1 component peaked on average at 0.078 s (SEM = 0.001) for UVF stimuli.
source: On stimulation trials, the C1 component peaked on average at 0.079 s (SEM = 0.001) and at 0.078 s (SEM = 0.001) for LVF and UVF stimuli respectively, with a maximum at occipito-parietal electrodes (Figure 2B, left and middle panels).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experimental data.

claim: The C1 component had a maximum at occipito-parietal electrodes.
source: On stimulation trials, the C1 component peaked on average at 0.079 s (SEM = 0.001) and at 0.078 s (SEM = 0.001) for LVF and UVF stimuli respectively, with a maximum at occipito-parietal electrodes (Figure 2B, left and middle panels).
evidence: This is a spatial characteristic of the C1 component observed in the data.

claim: The comparison of C1 amplitudes at individual peak electrodes on LVF (M = 10.157 μV; SEM = 0.918) and UVF (M = −10.567 μV; SEM = 1.058) trials revealed the expected polarity reversal.
source: The comparison of C1 amplitudes at individual peak electrodes on LVF (M = 10.157 μV ; SEM = 0.918) and UVF (M = −10.567 μV; SEM = 1.058) trials revealed the expected polarity reversal, confirming that this component originates from initial afferent activity in early visual areas (Di Russo et al., 2002; Di Russo et al., 2003; Bao et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data that confirms the C1 component's origin.

claim: The C1 polarity reversal confirms that this component originates from initial afferent activity in early visual areas.
source: The comparison of C1 amplitudes at individual peak electrodes on LVF (M = 10.157 μV ; SEM = 0.918) and UVF (M = −10.567 μV; SEM = 1.058) trials revealed the expected polarity reversal, confirming that this component originates from initial afferent activity in early visual areas (Di Russo et al., 2002; Di Russo et al., 2003; Bao et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the polarity reversal finding, supported by citations.

claim: Following the C1, a N150 component was observed peaking between 0.100 and 0.200 s relative to stimulus onset.
source: Following the C1, we observed a N150 component peaking between 0.100 and 0.200 s relative to stimulus onset, with an occipital topography and a consistently negative polarity for both LVF and UVF stimuli.
evidence: This is a descriptive finding from the ERP data.

claim: The N150 component had an occipital topography and a consistently negative polarity for both LVF and UVF stimuli.
source: Following the C1, we observed a N150 component peaking between 0.100 and 0.200 s relative to stimulus onset, with an occipital topography and a consistently negative polarity for both LVF and UVF stimuli.
evidence: This is a descriptive finding about the spatial and polarity characteristics of the N150.

claim: The N150 was followed by a late deflection in the time range between 0.200 and 0.600 s relative to stimulus onset, with a parietal topography and consistent positive polarity for both LVF and UVF stimuli.
source: The N150 was followed by a late deflection in the time range between 0.200 and 0.600 s relative to stimulus onset, with a parietal topography and consistent positive polarity for both LVF and UVF stimuli.
evidence: This is a descriptive finding about the late ERP component.

claim: On Fix trials no C1 and N150 components were detected in the ERP at individual C1-peak electrodes for LVF and UVF stimuli (mean amplitude in the C1 time window: −0.044 μV, SEM = 0.196).
source: As expected, on Fix trials no C1 and N150 components were detected in the ERP at individual C1-peak electrodes for LVF and UVF stimuli (mean amplitude in the C1 time window: −0.044 μV, SEM = 0.196).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding showing the absence of early components on fixation-only trials.

claim: Fix trials showed a late positive deflection with similar timing and topography as on stimulation trials.
source: Fix trials showed a late positive deflection with similar timing and topography as on stimulation trials (Figure 2B, right panel).
evidence: This is a comparative finding between Fix and stimulation trials.

claim: On LVF trials, the statistical test revealed a negative cluster (p<0.001) indicating ERD, spanning time points from 0 to 0.900 s relative to stimulus onset, frequencies between 6 and 30 Hz, and all 64 electrodes.
source: On LVF trials, the statistical test revealed a negative cluster (p<0.001) indicating ERD, spanning time points from 0 to 0.900 s relative to stimulus onset, frequencies between 6 and 30 Hz, and all 64 electrodes (Figure 2C, left panel).
evidence: This is a statistical finding about event-related desynchronization.

source: The most negative t-statistic was found at 20 Hz, 0.234 s, and at electrode P7.
evidence: This is a specific statistical result identifying the peak ERD effect.

source: A positive cluster (p=0.041) indicating ERS spanned time points from 0 to 0.900 s relative to stimulus onset, frequencies between 5 and 8 Hz, and all 64 electrodes.
evidence: This is a statistical finding about event-related synchronization.

source: The most positive t-statistic was found at 5 Hz, 0.097 s, and at electrode P7.

source: On UVF trials, the statistical test revealed a negative cluster (p<0.001) indicating ERD, spanning time points from 0 to 0.900 s relative to stimulus onset, frequencies between 6 and 30 Hz, and all 64 electrodes (Figure 2C, middle panel).

source: This test also found two positive clusters indicating ERS. The first positive cluster (p=0.032) spanned time points from 0 to 0.900 s relative to stimulus onset, frequencies between 5 and 8 Hz, and all 64 electrodes.

source: The second positive cluster (p=0.034) spanned time points from 0.49 to 0.900 s relative to stimulus onset, frequencies between 13 and 30 Hz, and 62 electrodes.

source: For Fix trials, the statistical test revealed one negative cluster (p<0.001) indicating ERD, spanning time points from 0 to 0.900 s relative to fixation-target onset, frequencies between 5 and 30 Hz, and all 64 electrodes (Figure 2C, right panel).

source: On LVF trials, a statistical test comparing ERP amplitudes during the early time window (<0.200 s) on trials with strong vs weak prestimulus power found a significant negative cluster (p=0.015).
evidence: This is a statistical finding about the effect of prestimulus power on early ERP components.

claim: The negative cluster on LVF trials indicates that the ERP amplitude in a time range containing the C1 (0.043 to 0.121 s) was weaker (i.e., less positive) on trials with strong prestimulus power between 8 and 28 Hz, and at all 64 electrodes.
source: This indicates that the ERP amplitude in a time range containing the C1 (0.043 to 0.121 s) was weaker (i.e., less positive) on trials with strong prestimulus power between 8 and 28 Hz, and at all 64 electrodes (Figure 3A, left panel).

source: The most negative t-statistic was found at 10 Hz, 0.078 s, and at electrode P4 (t(23)=−6.030).

claim: At the time-frequency-electrode point of most negative t-statistic for C1 on LVF trials, this effect was corroborated by the aperiodic-adjusted analysis (t(23)=−3.634; FDR-corrected p=0.003).
source: At this time-frequency-electrode point, this effect was corroborated by the aperiodic-adjusted analysis (t(23)=−3.634; FDR-corrected p=0.003), demonstrating that the ERP amplitude was indeed modulated by oscillatory power (Appendix 1—figure 1C).

source: At this time-frequency-electrode point, this effect was corroborated by the aperiodic-adjusted analysis (t(23)=−3.634; FDR-corrected p=0.003), demonstrating that the ERP amplitude was indeed modulated by oscillatory power (Appendix 1—figure 1C).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the aperiodic-adjusted analysis results.

source: Furthermore, the statistical test revealed a significant positive cluster (p<0.001), indicating that the ERP amplitude in a time range containing the N150 (0.090 to 0.200 s) was weaker (i.e., less negative) on trials with strong prestimulus power between 5 and 24 Hz, and at all 64 electrodes (Figure 3A, left panel).

source: The most positive t-statistic was found at 9 Hz, 0.145 ms, and at electrode P1 (total-band power: t(23)=7.940; aperiodic-adjusted power: t(23)=5.381; FDR-corrected p<0.001, Appendix 1—figure 1C).

source: The first cluster (p<0.001) indicated that the ERP amplitude in a time range containing the C1 (0.02 to 0.113 s) was weaker (i.e., less negative) on trials with strong prestimulus power between 5 and 22 Hz, and at all 64 electrodes (Figure 3A, middle panel).

source: The most positive t-statistic was found at 13 Hz, 0.082 ms, and at electrode PO4 (total-band power: t(23)=8.365; aperiodic-adjusted power: t(23)=2.315; FDR-corrected p=0.045, Appendix 1—figure 1C).

source: The second cluster indicated that the ERP amplitude in a time range containing the N150 (0.125 to 0.200 s) was weaker (i.e., less negative) on trials with strong prestimulus power between 5 and 25 Hz, and at all 64 electrodes.

source: The most positive t-statistic was found at 10 Hz, 0.168 ms, and at electrode F2 (total-band power: t(23)=8.544; aperiodic-adjusted power: t(23)=5.785; FDR-corrected p<0.001, Appendix 1—figure 1C).

claim: The results on early ERP components show that ERP amplitude on stimulation trials is attenuated during states of strong prestimulus power, regardless of the polarity of the components.
source: Taken together, the results on early ERP components show that ERP amplitude on stimulation trials is attenuated during states of strong prestimulus power, regardless of the polarity of the components.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the findings on early ERP components.

claim: The attenuation of early ERP amplitude by strong prestimulus power provides evidence for the functional inhibition mechanism.
source: This provides evidence for the functional inhibition mechanism underlying the modulatory effect of prestimulus power on the early ERP components.

claim: The positive polarity of the late ERP component is expected as a result of ERD of oscillations with a negative mean.

source: The statistical test on UVF trials revealed two significant positive clusters, indicating that the late ERP (cluster 1: 0.336–0.900 s; cluster 2: 0.200–0.328 s) was greater during states of strong ERD at frequencies between 5 and 30 Hz, and at all 64 electrodes (Figure 5A/B, middle panel).

claim: States of stronger ERD were associated with a more positive deflection of the late ERP component, consistent with the baseline-shift account.
source: Taken together, these results show that states of stronger ERD were associated with a more positive deflection of the late ERP component, consistent with the baseline-shift account.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the ERD-late ERP findings.

claim: Strong low-frequency prestimulus oscillations were associated with strong ERD in all trial types.
source: We found that strong low-frequency prestimulus oscillations were associated with strong ERD in all trial types (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a finding about the relationship between prestimulus power and ERD magnitude.

claim: On LVF trials, the significant positive cluster (p<0.001) for the prestimulus power-late ERP relationship spanned time points from 0.402 to 0.900 s, frequencies between 5 and 25 Hz, and all 64 electrodes.
source: On LVF trials, the significant positive cluster (p<0.001) spanned time points from 0.402 to 0.900 s, frequencies between 5 and 25 Hz, and all 64 electrodes (Figure 3A/B, left panel).
evidence: This is a statistical finding about the effect of prestimulus power on late ERP amplitude.

claim: The most positive t-statistic for the prestimulus power-late ERP relationship on LVF trials was found at 11 Hz, 0.676 s, and at electrode POz (total-band power: t(23)=6.769; aperiodic-adjusted power: t(23)=3.004; FDR-corrected p=0.014).
source: The most positive t-statistic was found at 11 Hz, 0.676 s, and at electrode POz (total-band power: t(23)=6.769; aperiodic-adjusted power: t(23)=3.004; FDR-corrected p=0.014, Appendix 1—figure 1C).
evidence: This is a specific statistical result for the prestimulus power-late ERP relationship on LVF trials.

claim: On UVF trials, the significant positive cluster (p=0.004) for the prestimulus power-late ERP relationship spanned time points from 0.445 to 0.900 s relative to stimulus onset, frequencies between 5 and 15 Hz, and all 64 electrodes.
source: On UVF trials, the significant positive cluster (p=0.004) spanned time points from 0.445 to 0.900 s relative to stimulus onset, frequencies between 5 and 15 Hz, and all 64 electrodes (Figure 3A/B, middle panel).
evidence: This is a statistical finding about the prestimulus power-late ERP relationship on UVF trials.

claim: The most positive t-statistic for the prestimulus power-late ERP relationship on UVF trials was found at 5 Hz, 0.648 s, and at electrode CP1 (total-band power: t(23)=7.600; aperiodic-adjusted power: t(23)=2.528; FDR-corrected p=0.037).
source: The most positive t-statistic was found at 5 Hz, 0.648 s, and at electrode CP1 (total-band power: t(23)=7.600; aperiodic-adjusted power: t(23)=2.528; FDR-corrected p=0.037, Appendix 1—figure 1C).
evidence: This is a specific statistical result for UVF trials.

claim: On Fix trials, the significant positive cluster (p<0.001) for the prestimulus power-late ERP relationship spanned time points from 0.484 to 0.900 s relative to fixation-target onset, frequencies between 5 and 23 Hz, and all 64 electrodes.
source: On Fix trials, the significant positive cluster (p<0.001) spanned time points from 0.484 to 0.900 s relative to fixation-target onset, frequencies between 5 and 23 Hz, and all 64 electrodes (Figure 3A/B, right panel).
evidence: This is a statistical finding about the prestimulus power-late ERP relationship on fixation-only trials.

claim: The most positive t-statistic for the prestimulus power-late ERP relationship on Fix trials was found at 7 Hz, 0.781 s, and at electrode POz (total-band power: t(23)=7.528; aperiodic-adjusted power: t(23)=1.881; FDR-corrected p=0.109).
source: The most positive t-statistic was found at 7 Hz, 0.781 s, and at electrode POz (total-band power: t(23)=7.528; aperiodic-adjusted power: t(23)=1.881; FDR-corrected p=0.109, Appendix 1—figure 1C).
evidence: This is a specific statistical result for Fix trials.

claim: The late ERP component is generated by a baseline shift during the ERD of non-zero mean oscillations.
source: Taken together, these results show that: (1) the late ERP component is generated by a baseline shift during the ERD of non-zero mean oscillations; (2) states of strong prestimulus power are followed by strong ERD, which manifests as an enhancement of the late ERP component.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple lines of evidence.

claim: States of strong prestimulus power are followed by strong ERD, which manifests as an enhancement of the late ERP component.
source: Taken together, these results show that: (1) the late ERP component is generated by a baseline shift during the ERD of non-zero mean oscillations; (2) states of strong prestimulus power are followed by strong ERD, which manifests as an enhancement of the late ERP component.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion linking prestimulus power to ERD and late ERP amplitude.

claim: Significant positive clusters were found for frequencies below 18 Hz and with a widespread topography in each trial type, indicating that the stronger the prestimulus power, the higher the subjective sleepiness.
source: We found significant positive clusters for frequencies below 18 Hz and with a widespread topography in each trial type (Appendix 1—figure 2A). This result indicates that the stronger the prestimulus power, the higher the subjective sleepiness.
evidence: This is a finding about the relationship between prestimulus power and sleepiness.

claim: The results of the re-analysis with sleepiness-corrected power estimates were virtually identical to the ones obtained with raw power estimates, suggesting that the effects observed were not confounded by sleepiness.
source: The results of this re-analysis (Appendix 1—figure 2B) were virtually identical to the ones obtained with raw power estimates (Figure 3A), suggesting that the effects we observed were not confounded by sleepiness.
evidence: This is a control analysis demonstrating that sleepiness does not confound the main findings.

claim: The results on the early ERP components in this study (<0.200 s: C1/N150) confirm and extend findings from past literature in the visual and auditory modalities.
source: The results on the early ERP components in this study (<0.200 s: C1/N150) confirm and extend findings from past literature in the visual and auditory modalities.
evidence: This is a statement about how the current findings relate to previous literature.

claim: A similar pattern of results was found for the N100 in the auditory modality.
source: A similar pattern of results was found for the N100 in the auditory modality (Başar and Stampfer, 1985; Jasiukaitis and Hakerem, 1988).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from previous auditory studies, supported by citations.

claim: Previous results that have been used to support the functional inhibition account could actually have been caused by a baseline shift.
source: It is important to note that previous results (e.g., Başar and Stampfer, 1985; Becker et al., 2008) that have been used to support the functional inhibition account could actually have been caused by a baseline shift.
evidence: This is a critical evaluation of previous interpretations, suggesting an alternative explanation.

claim: By showing that the absolute amplitude of the C1 component is diminished by stronger prestimulus power, regardless of polarity, we can rule out a baseline shift which would affect both polarities in the same direction.
source: In the current study, we leverage the fact that the C1 has a well-known polarity reversal as a function of the visual field of the stimulus. By showing that the absolute amplitude of the C1 component is diminished by stronger prestimulus power, regardless of polarity, we can rule out a baseline shift which would affect both polarities in the same direction (e.g, a net increase or decrease of voltage).
evidence: This is a methodological argument explaining how the study design rules out baseline shift as an explanation for early ERP effects.

claim: Previous results may have been due to fluctuations of the 1/f aperiodic signal or fluctuations of sleepiness.
source: Additionally, previous results may have also have been due to (1) fluctuations of the 1/f aperiodic signal (which affect total-band power estimates, see Appendix 1—figure 1), or (2) fluctuations of sleepiness (which affect both oscillatory power and ERP amplitude, see Appendix 1—figure 2).
evidence: This is a critical evaluation of potential confounds in previous studies.

claim: The current study confirmed that the early ERP amplitude was indeed reduced by oscillatory power, rather than just the 1/f aperiodic signal, and that this effect was not an epiphenomenon due to sleepiness.
source: In the current study, we confirmed that the early ERP amplitude was indeed reduced by oscillatory power, rather than just the 1/f aperiodic signal, and that this effect was not an epiphenomenon due to sleepiness.
evidence: This is a summary of control analyses that rule out confounds.

claim: These findings provide the first conclusive evidence for the functional inhibition effect of prestimulus oscillations on the early ERP amplitude.
source: Taken together, these findings provide the first conclusive evidence for the functional inhibition effect of prestimulus oscillations on the early ERP amplitude.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty and conclusiveness of the current findings.

claim: The relationship between prestimulus power and early ERP components in the somatosensory modality may be non-linear (inverted U-shaped) or vary across early components.
source: Unlike in the visual and auditory modality, the relationship between prestimulus power and early ERP components in the somatosensory modality (e.g., N1) may be non-linear (inverted U-shaped: Zhang and Ding, 2010; Ai and Ro, 2014; Forschack et al., 2017) or vary across early components (i.e., negative for M50 and positive for M70, P35 and P60: Jones et al., 2009; Nikouline et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from somatosensory studies, supported by citations.

claim: The relationship between prestimulus power and somatosensory perceptual performance has been found to have an inverted U-shape or to be linear.
source: Similarly, the relationship between prestimulus power and somatosensory perceptual performance has been found to have an inverted U-shape (Linkenkaer-Hansen et al., 2004), or to be linear (Haegens et al., 2011; Craddock et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a summary of findings on somatosensory perception, supported by citations.

claim: In the somatosensory domain distinct functional mechanisms may map onto low-frequency oscillations.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that in the somatosensory domain distinct functional mechanisms may map onto low-frequency oscillations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the variability of findings in the somatosensory domain.

claim: Some previous studies delivered visual stimuli to participants with eyes closed, which may explain inconsistencies with the current study.
source: First, some of these studies delivered visual stimuli to participants with eyes closed (Brandt and Jansen, 1991; Brandt and Jansen, 1991; Brandt, 1997; Jansen and Brandt, 1991). Instead, the majority of previous studies (including ours) delivered visual stimuli to participants with eyes open. It is known that oscillatory power in low frequencies has different spectral (Barry et al., 2007) and functional (Kaida et al., 2006) properties depending on whether subjects' eyes are open or closed; thus, these inconsistencies may be due to the eyes-open/closed difference.
evidence: This is an explanation for inconsistencies between studies, based on methodological differences.

claim: Oscillatory power in low frequencies has different spectral and functional properties depending on whether subjects' eyes are open or closed.
source: It is known that oscillatory power in low frequencies has different spectral (Barry et al., 2007) and functional (Kaida et al., 2006) properties depending on whether subjects' eyes are open or closed; thus, these inconsistencies may be due to the eyes-open/closed difference.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: Most previous studies only analyzed a narrow frequency band, few electrodes and a single time point, which may explain inconsistent effects.
source: Second, unlike our study, which analyzed a broad frequency band, 64 electrodes, and an extensive post-stimulus time window (0–0.900 s), most previous studies only analyzed a narrow frequency band, few electrodes and a single time point. Therefore, it is possible that the inconsistent effects in previous studies were due to this selective (and under-sampled) analysis of EEG data.
evidence: This is a methodological critique of previous studies.

claim: Studies have demonstrated that the effect of weak prestimulus α-band power on hit rates is not due to more accurate perception, but rather to a more liberal detection bias.
source: More recently, studies have demonstrated that this effect is not due to more accurate perception, but rather to a more liberal detection bias (Limbach and Corballis, 2016; Iemi et al., 2017; Craddock et al., 2017; Iemi and Busch, 2018) and a concomitant increase in confidence (Samaha et al., 2017b) and subjective visibility (Benwell et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a summary of more recent findings that reinterpret earlier results, supported by citations.

claim: A change in bias could be due to a change in the observer's deliberate decision strategy without any change in sensory processing (decision bias).
source: Specifically, a change in bias could be due to a change in the observer's deliberate decision strategy without any change in sensory processing (decision bias).
evidence: This is a theoretical explanation of one type of bias mechanism.

claim: A change in bias could be due to a change in the subjective appearance of stimuli (perceptual bias).
source: Alternatively, a change in bias could be due to a change in the subjective appearance of stimuli (perceptual bias): liberal perceptual bias during states of weak prestimulus power could result from increased neural excitability amplifying both neural responses to sensory stimuli (thereby increasing hit rates) and responses to noise (thereby increasing false alarm rates).
evidence: This is a theoretical explanation of an alternative bias mechanism.

claim: The finding that the C1 is amplified during states of weak prestimulus power indicates that even the earliest visual evoked responses are modulated by prestimulus oscillations.
source: Interestingly, the present finding that the C1 is amplified during states of weak prestimulus power, indicates that even the earliest visual evoked responses are modulated by prestimulus oscillations.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the C1 findings.

claim: The C1 finding supports a perceptual bias mechanism more than a decision bias mechanism.
source: Even though we could not study an equivalent amplification of responses to noise using the present paradigm, this finding supports a perceptual bias mechanism more than a decision bias mechanism.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the implications of the C1 findings for understanding bias mechanisms.

claim: It is possible that attention-related and spontaneous oscillations have different effects on the amplitude of the C1 component.
source: However, it is possible that attention-related and spontaneous oscillations have different effects on the amplitude of the C1 component.
evidence: This is a caveat about generalizing the current findings to attention-related oscillations.

claim: There are four requirements to demonstrate the baseline-shift mechanism.
source: There are four requirements to demonstrate the baseline-shift mechanism.
evidence: This is a statement of the methodological requirements for demonstrating the baseline-shift mechanism.

claim: The ongoing oscillations must have a non-zero mean (first requirement for baseline-shift mechanism).
source: First, the ongoing oscillations must have a non-zero mean.
evidence: This is the first requirement for demonstrating baseline shift.

claim: Sensory stimuli must modulate the amplitude of ongoing oscillations (second requirement for baseline-shift mechanism).
source: Second, sensory stimuli must modulate the amplitude of ongoing oscillations.
evidence: This is the second requirement for demonstrating baseline shift.

claim: The non-zero mean and the late ERP must have opposite polarity in case of ERD (third requirement for baseline-shift mechanism).
source: Third, the non-zero mean and the late ERP must have opposite polarity in case of ERD.
evidence: This is the third requirement for demonstrating baseline shift.

claim: ERD magnitude must correlate with the amplitude of the late ERP component (fourth requirement for baseline-shift mechanism).
source: Fourth, ERD magnitude must correlate with the amplitude of the late ERP component.
evidence: This is the fourth requirement for demonstrating baseline shift.

claim: A strong ERD was observed in frequencies between 6 and 30 Hz in all three trial types.
source: We observed a strong ERD in frequencies between 6 and 30 Hz in all three trial types.
evidence: This is a finding about event-related oscillations across trial types.

claim: On Fix trials there were no robust early evoked components due to the lack of strong visual input, yet an ERD was observed following the same spatio-temporal dynamics as on stimulation trials (though of a lesser magnitude).
source: On Fix trials there were no robust early evoked components due to the lack of strong visual input, yet we observed an ERD following the same spatio-temporal dynamics as on stimulation trials (though of a lesser magnitude).
evidence: This is a comparative finding between Fix and stimulation trials.

claim: In addition to the ERD, a strong ERS was observed below 8 Hz on stimulation trials (but not on Fix trials) possibly reflecting a leakage from the robust evoked components measured during the early time window.
source: In addition to the ERD, we also observed a strong ERS below 8 Hz on stimulation trials (but not on Fix trials) possibly reflecting a leakage from the robust evoked components measured during the early time window.
evidence: This is a finding about low-frequency ERS with a proposed explanation.

claim: Oscillations with a negative non-zero mean were associated with a late ERP component of positive polarity.
source: Consistent with this requirement, our results showed that oscillations with a negative non-zero mean were associated with a late ERP component of positive polarity.
evidence: This is a finding that confirms the third requirement of the baseline-shift mechanism.

claim: Strong ERD of non-zero mean oscillations was associated with enhanced ERP amplitude during the late time window.
source: Our results indicated that strong ERD of non-zero mean oscillations was associated with enhanced ERP amplitude during the late time window.
evidence: This is a finding that confirms the fourth requirement of the baseline-shift mechanism.

claim: The late ERP component was characterized by a topography and time-course similar to the ones of the ERD, consistent with Mazaheri and Jensen (2008).
source: Importantly, the late ERP component was characterized by a topography and time-course similar to the ones of the ERD, consistent with Mazaheri and Jensen (2008).
evidence: This is a finding about the similarity between late ERP and ERD characteristics, supported by a citation.

claim: These findings confirm the four requirements necessary to demonstrate the baseline-shift mechanism for the generation of the late ERP component.
source: In sum, these findings confirm the four requirements necessary to demonstrate the baseline-shift mechanism for the generation of the late ERP component.
evidence: This is a summary statement about meeting all requirements for the baseline-shift mechanism.

claim: Trials with strong prestimulus power were related to strong ERD magnitude, consistent with previous studies.
source: We found that trials with strong prestimulus power were related to strong ERD magnitude, consistent with previous studies (Min et al., 2007; Becker et al., 2008; Tenke et al., 2015; Benwell et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a finding about the relationship between prestimulus power and ERD, supported by citations.

claim: Due to circularity in the measures of ERD and prestimulus power, the statistical estimates of their relationship are inflated.
source: Due to circularity in these measures (i.e., ERD is computed with prestimulus power), the statistical estimates of this relationship are inflated.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a methodological limitation.

claim: The average prestimulus voltage is expected to differ between different prestimulus power bins due to the non-zero-mean property of neural oscillations.
source: Accordingly, whereas the average prestimulus voltage is expected to differ between different prestimulus power bins due to the non-zero-mean property of neural oscillations, the average post-stimulus voltage in the late window is expected to be the same regardless of prestimulus power (Figure 1B, upper panel).
evidence: This is a prediction based on the non-zero-mean property and the convergence of poststimulus power.

claim: The average post-stimulus voltage in the late window is expected to be the same regardless of prestimulus power.
source: Accordingly, whereas the average prestimulus voltage is expected to differ between different prestimulus power bins due to the non-zero-mean property of neural oscillations, the average post-stimulus voltage in the late window is expected to be the same regardless of prestimulus power (Figure 1B, upper panel).
evidence: This is a prediction based on the convergence of poststimulus power levels.

claim: The baseline-shift account predicts that subtracting a stronger prestimulus signal (strong power bin) yields a stronger shift of the EEG signal from the prestimulus baseline, and thus a stronger late ERP component.
source: The baseline-shift account predicts that subtracting a stronger prestimulus signal (strong power bin) yields a stronger shift of the EEG signal from the prestimulus baseline, and thus a stronger late ERP component (Figure 1B, lower panel).
evidence: This is a prediction of the baseline-shift account.

claim: A positive relationship was found between prestimulus power and the amplitude of the late ERP component.
source: Consistent with our prediction, we also found a positive relationship between prestimulus power and the amplitude of the late ERP component.
evidence: This is a finding that confirms the prediction of the baseline-shift account.

claim: These results confirm and extend previous findings in visual and auditory modalities.
source: These results confirm and extend previous findings in visual and auditory modalities.
evidence: This is a statement about how the current findings relate to previous literature.

claim: A similar pattern of results was found on late ERP components in the auditory modality.
source: A similar pattern of results was found on late ERP components in the auditory modality (0.250–0.800 s: Jasiukaitis and Hakerem, 1988; 0.400 s: Başar and Stampfer, 1985; 0.200–0.500 s: Barry et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from previous auditory studies, supported by citations.

claim: This study resolves the apparent inconsistency in previous literature by demonstrating that the positive relationship can be accounted for by the baseline-shift mechanism, rather than functional inhibition.
source: Therefore, this study resolves this apparent inconsistency in previous literature, by demonstrating that this positive relationship can be accounted for by the baseline-shift mechanism, rather than functional inhibition.
evidence: This is a claim about the contribution of the current study to resolving inconsistencies in the literature.

claim: While early ERP components are likely generated primarily through the additive mechanism (because ERD is negligible in this time window), late ERP components can have a contribution from both additive and baseline-shift mechanisms.
source: While early ERP components are likely generated primarily through the additive mechanism (because ERD is negligible in this time window), late ERP components can have a contribution from both additive and baseline-shift mechanisms.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement about the mechanisms underlying early vs. late ERP components.

claim: Functional inhibition of additive components in the initial part of the late time window might have canceled the amplification effect due to the baseline shift.
source: Functional inhibition of additive components in the initial part of the late time window might have canceled the amplification effect due to the baseline shift.
evidence: This is a proposed explanation for the timing of the prestimulus power effect on late ERP.

claim: This cancellation might explain the lack of a significant effect at the peak of the late component.
source: This cancellation might explain the lack of a significant effect at the peak of the late component.
evidence: This is a proposed explanation for a specific pattern in the results.

claim: The ERP during the later time window (>0.400 s) is more likely to show primarily baseline-shift-generated components and thus is more susceptible to the amplification effect of prestimulus power.
source: In contrast, the ERP during the later time window (>0.400 s) is more likely to show primarily baseline-shift-generated components and thus is more susceptible to the amplification effect of prestimulus power.
evidence: This is an explanation for why the prestimulus power effect is strongest in the later time window.

claim: The positive modulation of the late ERP component is directly produced by the modulation of ERD magnitude as a function of prestimulus power.
source: We conclude that the positive modulation of the late ERP component is directly produced by the modulation of ERD magnitude as a function of prestimulus power.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the mechanism underlying the late ERP effect.

claim: Previous results on the late ERP component may have been influenced by fluctuations of the 1/f aperiodic signal or fluctuations of sleepiness.
source: It is important to note that previous results on the late ERP component (e.g., Dockree et al., 2007; Becker et al., 2008) may have been influenced by (1) fluctuations of the 1/f aperiodic signal (which affect total-band power estimates, see Appendix 1—figure 1), or (2) fluctuations of sleepiness (which affect both oscillatory power and ERP amplitude, see Appendix 1—figure 2).
evidence: This is a critical evaluation of potential confounds in previous studies on late ERP.

claim: The current study confirmed that the late ERP amplitude was indeed amplified by oscillatory power, rather than just the 1/f aperiodic signal, and that this effect was not an epiphenomenon due to sleepiness.
source: In the current study, we confirmed that the late ERP amplitude was indeed amplified by oscillatory power, rather than just the 1/f aperiodic signal, and that this effect was not an epiphenomenon due to sleepiness.
evidence: This is a summary of control analyses for the late ERP findings.

claim: This provides the first evidence that the effect of prestimulus oscillations on the late ERP component is due to the mechanism of baseline shift.
source: This provides the first evidence that the effect of prestimulus oscillations on the late ERP component is due to the mechanism of baseline shift.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings on the baseline-shift mechanism.

claim: While the functional inhibition account describes a (proposed) physiological mechanism, the baseline-shift account describes an effect that is largely the consequence of specific properties of the signal and the way we analyze it.
source: It is important to highlight that, while the functional inhibition account describes a (proposed) physiological mechanism, the baseline-shift account describes an effect that is largely the consequence of specific properties of the signal and the way we analyze it.
evidence: This is a conceptual distinction between the two mechanisms.

claim: Baseline shift is a result of a combination of preconditions including signal properties (non-zero mean), the occurrence of an ERD, as well as conventional signal processing procedures (i.e., baseline correction).
source: That is, baseline shift is a result of a combination of preconditions including signal properties (non-zero mean), the occurrence of an ERD, as well as conventional signal processing procedures (i.e., baseline correction).
evidence: This is an explanation of the preconditions for baseline shift.

claim: The modulation of late responses predicted by a baseline shift can only exist if the preconditions (non-zero mean, ERD, baseline correction) are met.
source: The modulation of late responses predicted by a baseline shift can only exist if these preconditions are met, while the functional inhibition account generalizes to cases involving zero-mean oscillations, does not depend on the presence of an ERD, and can be established using different measures of brain activity (i.e., not limited to ERPs).
evidence: This is a statement about the conditional nature of baseline shift vs. the generality of functional inhibition.

claim: The functional inhibition account generalizes to cases involving zero-mean oscillations, does not depend on the presence of an ERD, and can be established using different measures of brain activity (i.e., not limited to ERPs).
source: The modulation of late responses predicted by a baseline shift can only exist if these preconditions are met, while the functional inhibition account generalizes to cases involving zero-mean oscillations, does not depend on the presence of an ERD, and can be established using different measures of brain activity (i.e., not limited to ERPs).
evidence: This is a statement about the broader applicability of the functional inhibition account.

claim: Some studies have proposed that the ERP can be generated by a reorganization of ongoing oscillations via phase reset.
source: In addition to these mechanisms, some studies have proposed that the ERP can be generated by a reorganization of ongoing oscillations via phase reset (Sayers et al., 1974; Makeig et al., 2002; Klimesch et al., 2004; Gruber et al., 2005; Fell et al., 2004; Fuentemilla et al., 2006; Hanslmayr et al., 2007; Sauseng et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a summary of an alternative theoretical account, supported by citations.

claim: According to the phase-reset account, the phases of ongoing oscillations are aligned (i.e., phase-reset) by the stimulus; as a consequence, averaging these phase-locked oscillations across trials does not lead to phase cancellation in the post-stimulus window, resulting in the generation of ERP components.
source: According to the phase-reset account, the phases of ongoing oscillations are aligned (i.e., phase-reset) by the stimulus; as a consequence, averaging these phase-locked oscillations across trials does not lead to phase cancellation in the post-stimulus window, resulting in the generation of ERP components.
evidence: This is an explanation of the phase-reset mechanism.

claim: It has been argued that phase reset in response to a stimulus can only occur if the oscillation already exists prior to the reset (i.e., during the prestimulus window).
source: On the one hand, it has been argued that phase reset in response to a stimulus can only occur if the oscillation already exists prior to the reset (i.e., during the prestimulus window).
evidence: This is a theoretical argument about the preconditions for phase reset.

claim: Any ERP component generated by phase reset is likely to be absent during desynchronized states (i.e., weakest power bin).
source: It follows that any ERP component generated by phase reset is likely to be absent during desynchronized states (i.e., weakest power bin) (Shah et al., 2004; Sauseng et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a prediction of the phase-reset account, supported by citations.

claim: Trials with weakest prestimulus power may result in less prominent phase reset, which would manifest as a reduction of the ERP amplitude.
source: This suggests that trials with weakest prestimulus power may result in less prominent phase reset, which would manifest as a reduction of the ERP amplitude.
evidence: This is a prediction of the phase-reset account.

claim: One can argue that strong oscillations represent a state with pronounced neuronal synchronization that is not easily affected by weak sensory inputs.
source: On the other hand, one can argue that strong oscillations represent a state with pronounced neuronal synchronization that is not easily affected by weak sensory inputs, as also shown in previous modeling work (Hansel and Sompolinsky, 1996).
evidence: This is an alternative theoretical argument about the effect of strong oscillations, supported by a citation.

claim: During states of strong ongoing oscillations, phase-reset may be harder to achieve and, consequently, is unlikely to result in ERP generation.
source: Thus, during states of strong ongoing oscillations, phase-reset may be harder to be achieved and, consequently, is unlikely to result in ERP generation.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the alternative argument about strong oscillations.

claim: This alternative phase-reset argument predicts an ERP attenuation by prestimulus power, consistent with the results during the early time window.
source: Accordingly, this predicts an ERP attenuation by prestimulus power, consistent with our results during the early time window.
evidence: This is a statement about consistency between an alternative phase-reset prediction and the current findings.

claim: In this study, it is difficult to distinguish whether the ERP attenuation affects ERP components generated by additive or phase-reset mechanisms.
source: It is worth noting that, in this study, it is difficult to distinguish whether this attenuation affects ERP components generated by additive or phase-reset mechanisms; invasive electrophysiological recordings allowing for higher spatial resolution might be required to address this particular question (Hanslmayr et al., 2007; Telenczuk et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation of the current study, with suggestions for future research.

claim: Regardless of the underlying mechanisms of ERP generation, the results during the early time window can be explained by the functional inhibition account.
source: Regardless of the underlying mechanisms of ERP generation, our results during the early time window can be explained by the functional inhibition account.
evidence: This is a statement about the robustness of the functional inhibition interpretation.

claim: This study demonstrates that spontaneous fluctuations of oscillatory brain activity modulate the amplitude of visual ERP via two distinct mechanisms: (1) functional inhibition of the early additive ERP components and (2) baseline shift affecting the late ERP component.
source: This study demonstrates that spontaneous fluctuations of oscillatory brain activity modulate the amplitude of visual ERP via two distinct mechanisms: (1) functional inhibition of the early additive ERP components and (2) baseline shift affecting the late ERP component.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: These findings show that neural oscillations have concurrent opposing effects on ERP generation.
source: Therefore, these findings show that neural oscillations have concurrent opposing effects on ERP generation.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the dual nature of oscillatory effects.

claim: Distinguishing between functional inhibition and baseline shift effects is crucial for understanding how neural oscillations control the processing of incoming sensory information in the brain.
source: Distinguishing between these effects is crucial for understanding how neural oscillations control the processing of incoming sensory information in the brain.
evidence: This is a statement about the importance of the findings.

claim: To ensure a robust estimate of the neurophysiological effect and account for potential missing data, a sample of 27 participants was recruited.
source: To ensure a robust estimate of our neurophysiological effect and account for potential missing data (e.g., due to artifacts), we recruited a larger sample of 27 participants (mean age: 26.33, SEM = 0.616; 14 females; three left-handed).
evidence: This is a methodological decision about sample size.

claim: All participants had normal or corrected-to-normal vision and no history of neurological disorders.
source: All participants had normal or corrected-to-normal vision and no history of neurological disorders.
evidence: This is a description of participant inclusion criteria.

claim: All experimental procedures were approved by the ethics committee of the German Psychological Society.
source: All experimental procedures were approved by the ethics committee of the German Psychological Society.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.

claim: Two participants were excluded before EEG preprocessing because of excessive artifacts.
source: Two participants were excluded before EEG preprocessing because of excessive artifacts.
evidence: This is information about participant exclusion.

claim: One participant was excluded after preprocessing because no C1 component could be detected.
source: One participant was excluded after preprocessing because no C1 component could be detected, unlike the rest of the sample.
evidence: This is information about participant exclusion based on data quality.

claim: A total of 24 participants were included in the analysis.
source: A total of 24 participants were included in the analysis.
evidence: This is the final sample size for the analysis.

claim: The C1 is described as the earliest component of the visual ERP with a peak latency between 0.055 and 0.09 s and an occipital topography.
source: The C1 is described as the earliest component of the visual ERP with a peak latency between 0.055 and 0.09 s and an occipital topography.
evidence: This is a description of the C1 component based on established knowledge.

claim: The C1 component is regarded as an index of initial afferent activity in primary visual cortex, because of its early latency and polarity reversal with reference to V1 anatomy.
source: The C1 component is regarded as an index of initial afferent activity in primary visual cortex, because of its early latency and polarity reversal with reference to V1 anatomy (Di Russo et al., 2002; Di Russo et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a statement about the functional significance of the C1, supported by citations.

claim: UVF and LVF stimulus positions were located at polar angles of 25° above and 45° below the horizontal meridian, respectively.
source: UVF and LVF stimulus positions were located at polar angles of 25° above and 45° below the horizontal meridian, respectively.
evidence: This is a description of the stimulus positions.

claim: These asymmetrical positions for UVF and LVF stimuli ensure a stimulation of primarily lower and upper banks of the calcarine fissure, respectively, resulting in a polarity reversal of scalp potentials.
source: These asymmetrical positions for UVF and LVF stimuli ensure a stimulation of primarily lower and upper banks of the calcarine fissure, respectively (Aine et al., 1996; Clark et al., 1994; Di Russo et al., 2002), resulting in a polarity reversal of scalp potentials.
evidence: This is an explanation of the rationale for the stimulus positions, supported by citations.

claim: A positive C1 component is obtained by LVF stimulation, while a negative C1 component is obtained by UVF stimulation.
source: A positive C1 component is obtained by LVF stimulation, while a negative C1 component is obtained by UVF stimulation (Di Russo et al., 2002; Di Russo et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a statement about the expected polarity of the C1 based on stimulus location, supported by citations.

claim: Mean accuracy in the fixation task was 94.85% (SEM = 0.0109) and did not significantly differ between trial types (p>0.05), indicating that participants were able to maintain central fixation.
source: Mean accuracy in the fixation task was 94.85% (SEM = 0.0109) and did not significantly differ between trial types (p>0.05), indicating that participants were able to maintain central fixation.
evidence: This is a behavioral finding demonstrating task compliance.

claim: Incorrect trials were discarded from further analysis (mean = 41; SEM = 8.620).
source: Incorrect trials were discarded from further analysis (mean = 41; SEM = 8.620).
evidence: This is information about data exclusion.

claim: On average 761 (SEM = 9.824) trials per participant were analyzed.
source: On average we analyzed 761 (SEM = 9.824) trials per participant.
